entry.title: A digital twin of the house, and teaching the robot in it
entry.summary: I built a copy of the house in NVIDIA Isaac Sim where the robot's real software drives a simulated Roomba. How it was generated (it isn't an AI turning a video into a house), what it has already caught, and where I'm going next: developing navigation algorithms in Isaac Lab.
entry.content:
Testing a robot in the real house means moving furniture, waiting for people to walk past and hoping it doesn't fall down the stairs. So the robot now has a digital twin: a copy of the house on my PC where a simulated Roomba, with the same camera, is driven by the robot's real software. I can run it all night, break things on purpose and watch exactly what the robot sees and decides.

Two twins

  • A 2D twin for speed. The real driver, Nav2, the explorer and obstacle detection run against a flat simulated house and Roomba. Nine scripted scenarios, such as starting nose to a wall, a door closing mid-run, an invisible railing, low battery and a person walking through, are scored automatically: area covered, bumps, stuck episodes and how the run ended.
  • A 3D twin in NVIDIA Isaac Sim for realism. The full stack (visual odometry, 3D mapping, Nav2, the explorer and the person detector) runs in Linux on the PC and drives the Roomba through the same serial protocol as the real one. Isaac Sim renders the camera, depth and IMU at the real rates, with simulated people walking around.

How the house was generated

It would be nice to say an AI watched a video and produced a finished house. That's not what happened. It's a semi-automated, procedural reconstruction: the floor plans supply clean structure, the robot's own recordings supply measured geometry and alignment, and Python builds the rest. Anything nobody measured is an educated guess.

1. The robot's own scan

The first attempt used the map the robot already had. From a recorded drive, RTAB-Map exported a point cloud, the 2D occupancy grid and a textured mesh made with Poisson surface reconstruction. It loaded, but it looked like a cave: holes wherever the camera never looked, a bumpy floor, and long stretched triangles where the mesh bridged gaps. A camera 13 cm off the floor simply doesn't see the tops of things.

2. The floor plans

The plans had exactly what the scan lacked: straight walls and every door, window and step. OpenCV picks out the plan's thick black wall lines, curves and diagonals included. Rooms, doors (with the side they swing to), windows, stairs, railings and fixtures were digitised into JSON, then reviewed and completed by hand. The room dimensions printed on the plan set the scale; across eight rooms they agreed to within 0.4 %.

3. Lining it up with the map

A plan is a drawing; the robot's map is in metres, in its own frame. A search tries every rotation (and the mirror image) and slides the plan around to find where its walls best overlap the mapped walls, then ICP refines the fit. The median plan wall ends up within about 10 cm of a mapped one, and 97 % of the robot's recorded path lands on plan floor. The rebuilt house and the robot's real drives now share one coordinate system. The robot has only mapped one floor, so the other was stacked under it from its own plan, using the staircase to line the two up.

4. Building it in Python

From the aligned plan, a script generates extruded walls, floors, ceilings, door frames and doors, stairs, railings, materials and lights. Furniture is a mix: where the robot mapped an obstacle inside a room, a piece with that footprint goes there; elsewhere come procedural pieces and models from an asset library. The beds and dressers are stand-ins in roughly the right places, not copies of ours.

5. Into Isaac Sim

The house is exported as OpenUSD with collision geometry and loaded into Isaac Sim with a Roomba model whose frames match the real robot. The simulated cameras use the real calibration, down to the 11.8 cm stereo baseline and the 13 cm lens height. One bug worth recording: each room's floor started as a separate box, and the physics engine snagged the caster on the seams, stopping the robot dead at doorways. One welded floor mesh fixed it.

Measured, drawn or guessed

Measured: wall positions where the robot has been, the scale, the robot's path and the camera calibration. From the plans: the layout, doors, windows and stairs. Approximated: anything the robot never saw, most of the furniture, and wall and ceiling heights. A few doorways sit 10–30 cm from where the map puts them, and the simulated robot gets stuck in exactly those spots.

What it has caught so far

The point of a twin is finding problems before the real robot does. The 2D scenarios turned up seven, and most were logic bugs rather than anything a smarter algorithm would fix:

  • Trapping itself: a bump keep-out mark could cover the robot, leaving it nowhere to go.
  • Skipping rooms: reachable areas were written off by a hard distance cutoff.
  • Giving up early: it could declare the house finished without a final look around, and areas blocked by a closed door or a passing person were never rechecked.
  • Ending elsewhere: runs didn't always finish back at the start, and Nav2 could hang at start-up.

Each fix is checked with before-and-after runs of every scenario. The depth view in the clip shows the other recurring problem: anything closer than 0.3 m is black to the camera, so a wall right in front of the robot is invisible.

Where I'm going next

This is where the project turns for me. So far most of the work has been getting a 2007 Roomba to see, map and drive at all. Next, I'm going to spend my time developing navigation algorithms of my own in NVIDIA Isaac Lab, which runs on top of Isaac Sim and teaches behaviours by trial and error (reinforcement learning) with thousands of simulated robots at once on the RTX 5090. Nav2 keeps planning the actual routes; these are the parts I want to fix:

ProblemTodayWhat I'll try
Getting unstuckSpin, back up, clear the map, waitA learned recovery skill (training now)
Where to exploreNearest unexplored edgeA learned chooser that also weighs unknown area, route risk and visit order
Thin railingsJoin the posts the camera sees into a wallSpot railings in the camera image, trained on simulated ones
CleaningNot yetCover the rooms I pick with the least driving, and know when it's done

First up: getting unstuck

The learned version practises on 4,096 simulated Roombas at a time, each starting stuck in a different 4 × 4 m situation generated in code: nose to a wall inside the camera's blind zone, wedged in a corner, between chair legs, under a shelf at camera height, at a railing the camera can't see, or boxed in by its own bump marks.

It sees only what the real robot has at that moment: the nearby costmap, the light bumpers and bump switches, wheel speeds, the gyro, how far it has moved recently and where it was trying to go. It answers with a forward speed and a turn rate. It's rewarded for getting clear and making progress towards its goal, and penalised for bumps, scraping the camera on overhangs, drops, jerky moves and wasted time. Every command still passes through the same safety layers as on the robot: the speed limits, the collision monitor and the driver's bump and cliff reflexes.

The rule

Every idea gets the same treatment: design the situations it practises on, the rewards and the tests, train it on the 5090, and race it against the classical logic in both twins, on situations it never trained on. Only the winners move to the Jetson, running from the Rust nodes, and the collision monitor and the bump and cliff reflexes always stay in charge of safety. The real house gets the final say.

The code: the 3D twin, including the house builder, is in twin/isaac, and the 2D twin's nine scenarios are in config/twin2d.

entry.title: From Python to Rust: same robot, a fraction of the CPU
entry.summary: Ten of the robot's ROS 2 nodes now have Rust versions, each checked against the Python original output for output. The five busiest went from about 1.3 CPU cores to under a fifth of one.
entry.content:
The Jetson was working too hard. On a typical exploration run its load average sat around 20 on six cores: far more work waiting than it had cores to run it on. Most of the heavy lifting was already native code: Nav2 and RTAB-Map are C++, and cuVSLAM and nvblox run on the GPU. The overhead was in the glue I'd written myself in Python. The web dashboard, the Roomba driver, the odometry watchdog and the obstacle detector each used a quarter to a half of a CPU core.

So the rule for this project is now Rust wherever it's practical. Rather than redesign anything, each Python node gets a Rust twin that is a drop-in replacement: same node name, topics, parameters, services and even log lines. One launch argument, rust_nodes, picks which set runs.

The results

CPU use is in percent of one core, measured on the Jetson with both versions running side by side on the same input:

NodePythonRust
Web dashboard server48%10%
Roomba driver31%2.4%
Odometry watchdog26%2.2%
Floor obstacles19%2.5%
Wheel and gyro prep for the EKF8.7%1.2%
Explorer and nav coachRust uses about a sixth

Add up the first five and they went from about 132% of a core to 18%, giving back more than a whole core. Memory dropped too: the dashboard server peaks at 42 MB instead of 165 MB, and the driver and the watchdog at under 30 MB instead of about 75 MB.

The person detector, which finds people in the camera image with a TensorRT network on the GPU and works out how far away they are, is measured per camera frame instead. Its CPU time per frame fell from 45 to 13 ms, the median time from frame to result from 56 to 42 ms, and its memory from 649 to 448 MB. The map gap filler and the keep-out zones node were ported as well, so ten nodes now have Rust versions.

Same output, or it doesn't ship

Faster is easy to claim. The hard rule was that every Rust node has to give exactly the same output as the Python one, and that has to be proven, not eyeballed. Each port came with a test that feeds both versions identical input and compares everything they send out:

  • Odometry watchdog: a 35-minute recorded drive (413,000 IMU samples and 30,700 camera poses) through both. Both forwarded the same 26,084 poses, made the same 87 recoveries and printed the same 577 log lines. The largest difference in any position was about 0.000000000003 m. The same check passed on 17 runs, including injected faults such as tracking loss and a slow reset.
  • Map gap filler: 1,467 recorded and made-up maps, 23.5 million cells, identical.
  • Explorer: the same goals on 572 maps from real drives, including the bump keep-out marks and retries.
  • Person detector: 10,579 recorded frames, identical detections, distances and annotated images, down to the bytes of the JPEG.
  • Roomba driver: a fake Roomba on a virtual serial port, with scripted bumps, cliffs, bad checksums and dropped streams. Both drivers sent the robot exactly the same bytes.

Identical is harder than it sounds

Python, NumPy and OpenCV each have their own quirks, and matching them bit for bit meant copying them on purpose:

  • Rounding: to two decimal places, NumPy rounds 2.675 to 2.68, while Python's own round gives 2.67. The Rust code has to know which one the Python called.
  • Distances: Python's math.hypot is not the C library's hypot; for some inputs they differ in the last bit. That's enough to nudge a decision the other way.
  • Order matters: OpenCV numbers connected blobs in a particular order and NumPy sorts with a particular algorithm. Both had to be reproduced, or ties came out differently.
  • Missing pieces: ROS 2's Rust library has no TF (the transforms between the robot's coordinate frames), so it got a port of ROS's own that gives bit-identical results. NVIDIA ships no Rust bindings for cuVSLAM's messages either, so those are generated from the message definitions.
  • The linker: the standard Linux linker took over ten minutes to link one node on the Jetson. Switching to mold fixed that.

Not on the road yet

Every number here comes from recorded drives and a simulated Roomba. The Rust nodes are now the default, so the next real drive will be the first on Rust. If anything misbehaves, rust_nodes:=false brings back the Python versions.

The code: the Rust nodes are in src/roomba_rs, and the Python-vs-Rust comparison tools in tools/.

entry.title: Basalt vs cuVSLAM, round one: CPU or GPU?
entry.summary: The robot can work out how it's moving with Basalt on the CPU or NVIDIA cuVSLAM on the GPU. The GPU holds still better; Basalt stays on track better once it moves. Here's the scorecard so far.
entry.content:
The robot now has two ways to work out how it's moving. Basalt runs on the Jetson's CPU and NVIDIA cuVSLAM runs on its GPU. Both watch the same stereo camera and IMU, and one launch argument picks which one is in charge. That makes for a fair fight: I can record a run once and replay exactly the same camera frames through each.

The side-by-side maps are still to come, but the early numbers already tell an interesting story: the GPU is not simply better.

The scorecard so far

TestBasalt (CPU)cuVSLAM (GPU)Better
Parked 60 s: apparent drift0.9 cm0.3 cmGPU
Walk: jumps over 0.5 mNone16CPU
Walk: height drift10× less10× moreCPU
Loop-closure check it allowsStrict (25)Lenient (15)CPU
Processor loadBusy CPUMostly GPURound two

Standing still: the GPU wins

The simplest honest test is to park the robot and ask it how far it has moved. The right answer is zero. Over a minute, the CPU pipeline thought the robot had crept 0.9 cm and the GPU pipeline 0.3 cm. Fuse the calibrated wheels into the GPU pipeline's filter and it drops to 0.07 cm, as I found in the last post.

On the move: Basalt wins

Parking is the easy case. For the hard one, I carried the camera around the house, recorded everything it saw, and replayed the recording through both.

A jump is when the odometry suddenly decides the camera has teleported more than half a metre. The watchdog catches those so they never reach the map, but each one is a moment when the robot doesn't really know where it is. Basalt had none. cuVSLAM had 16, and its idea of the camera's height drifted about ten times as far as Basalt's. On the robot, cuVSLAM is told to stay in the floor plane, so height drift matters less there, but it's a good sign of how well each one is really tracking.

It started at 544

The first replay through cuVSLAM was a disaster: 544 jumps and 260 km of imagined travel in four minutes. Its default IMU settings are tuned for Intel RealSense cameras and trusted this camera's IMU far too much, so ordinary sensor noise looked like real motion. Telling it the IMU is ten times noisier brought that down to 16 jumps, and the number of times the watchdog caught vision disagreeing with the gyro fell from 157 to 31.

Why the map cares

Drift is what loop closure has to clean up. When RTAB-Map recognises a place it has seen before, it checks the match by counting the features both views share, then pulls the map straight.

With cuVSLAM, the corrections were big enough that I had to loosen that check to 15 matching features and tell RTAB-Map the odometry was less certain. Otherwise it rejected real loop closures, including one that needed a 7° correction. With Basalt, that loose check became a liability: similar-looking doors matched the wrong place and warped the map. Raising it to 25 gave a clean map on the same walk. Better odometry lets the map be pickier, and being picky is what keeps it straight.

So which one drives?

For now, Basalt. Staying on track while moving matters more than holding still, so the CPU pipeline is still the robot's default. The GPU pipeline is staying too: it takes the load off the CPU, and with the wheels fused in, it's the steadiest when parked. One launch argument switches between them.

Round two: maps

Numbers are nice; maps you can overlay are better. The next test replays one recorded drive through both pipelines, each building its own map from scratch, with the robot's drivers switched off so nothing can move. It counts tracking losses and loop closures, measures the map's area, and checks how far from the start each one thinks the robot finished. If the drive ends where it began, the right answer is zero. It also records how hard each one works the CPU and GPU. The test is compare_pipelines.sh.

entry.title: Moving the brains to the GPU: cuVSLAM, nvblox and sensor fusion
entry.summary: NVIDIA cuVSLAM for visual odometry, an EKF that fuses calibrated wheels, gyro and vision, and nvblox for obstacle mapping, all on the Jetson's GPU. Plus a frozen node, a smeared costmap and a new bump reflex.
entry.content:
The CPU pipeline from the last navigation post works, but it keeps the Jetson's six CPU cores busy while its GPU mostly sits there. This week I moved the heavy lifting onto the GPU and rebuilt how the robot works out where it is.

The new stack

  • NVIDIA cuVSLAM replaces Basalt for visual odometry. Same job (estimate motion from the stereo cameras and IMU), but on the GPU.
  • robot_localization runs an extended Kalman filter (EKF) that fuses every motion source into one best estimate.
  • nvblox builds a 3D model of nearby obstacles from the depth camera, on the GPU, and turns it into a costmap for Nav2.

Fusing wheels, gyro and vision

An EKF is only as good as what you tell it about each sensor, so I calibrated each input before letting it in:

  • Wheel speed, with measured correction factors: forward distance × 0.952 and rotation × 0.71. That second number is the carpet scrub from last time, now measured and corrected.
  • The camera's gyro, using noise figures from a three-hour stationary IMU recording and a measured static gyro bias, so the filter knows exactly how much to trust it.
  • Visual odometry, fused differentially. The filter uses the change in the VIO pose between updates rather than the pose itself. If cuVSLAM loses tracking and resets, it can't teleport the robot across the room.

Results: standing still

The simplest honest test is to park the robot and watch how far it thinks it has moved:

PipelineTestApparent drift
CPU (Basalt)Parked, 60 s0.9 cm
GPU (cuVSLAM)Parked, 60 s0.3 cm
GPU + wheels in the EKFParked, 30 s0.07 cm, 0.03°

Standing still is the easy case, of course. The real test is driving, which is next.

What went wrong (and got fixed)

The costmap that walled the robot in

I first added nvblox's obstacles to both of Nav2's costmaps. In the global costmap, which lives in the map frame, its marks never cleared, and every time RTAB-Map corrected the map they smeared sideways. After a few minutes the robot was surrounded by phantom walls. Now nvblox only feeds the local costmap, a small window that rolls along with the robot and is rebuilt constantly.

The node that froze mid-drive

Halfway through a test drive, my floor-obstacle node stopped publishing. The cause was a race between a ROS 2 TF listener's background thread and my own code. The good news: the collision monitor noticed the missing data and stopped the robot, exactly as designed. The race is fixed, and I trust that safety layer a lot more now.

A bump reflex

When the bumper does trigger, the robot now has a reflex: back up about 8 cm and turn away, before the planner tries again. It's a small thing that makes it look a lot less stuck.

Faster storage

Recording stereo images, depth and every sensor topic eats disk bandwidth. I swapped in a faster 256 GB NVMe drive, which manages about 1.8 GB/s on the Jetson's PCIe Gen3 x4 slot.

The code: vslam.launch.py starts cuVSLAM and the EKF; their settings, and nvblox's, are in ekf_robot.yaml and nvblox_robot.yaml.

Next

Next: the CPU (Basalt) and GPU (cuVSLAM) pipelines head to head. The first results, and why the GPU isn't simply better, are in Basalt vs cuVSLAM, round one.

entry.title: Powering it with a Ridgid 18 V tool battery
entry.summary: With charging out of action, the robot now runs on a Ridgid power-tool battery through a fuse and a 15 V regulator. Plus: why the Roomba's fuel gauge started lying, and the voltage monitor that will replace it.
entry.content:
With the Roomba unable to charge its own battery (see Charging Error 3), I needed another way to keep it running. Ridgid 18 V lithium-ion tool batteries were already part of my workshop, along with a charger that knows exactly how to look after them. That's a lot of well-managed energy sitting around doing nothing.

The power path

A full Ridgid pack sits around 20–21 V and sags towards 15 V as it empties. That's more than the Roomba ever sees from its own NiMH pack when full, and it changes as the pack drains, so a 15 V / 12 A buck regulator turns it into one steady voltage. 15 V sits comfortably inside the Roomba's normal battery range and inside the Jetson's 9–20 V input.

The regulator's output is soldered to the Roomba's battery contacts, so the robot thinks it has a battery, and also feeds the Jetson's barrel jack. A 7.5 A blade fuse goes right at the pack, before anything else. A lithium tool battery can deliver a frightening amount of current into a short circuit; the fuse makes sure a pinched wire is a blown fuse, not a fire.

Don't dock it like this

In this configuration the robot must never go back to its dock or have its charger plugged in. The charger would be pushing current into a regulator output and a lithium pack that it knows nothing about.

The fuel gauge that lied

The Roomba estimates its charge by counting the current flowing in and out of its own NiMH pack. Feed it from somewhere else and that number means nothing. During one test drive, on a freshly charged Ridgid pack, it decided it was at 20% and headed home to its dock, which is precisely the one thing it mustn't do now.

So the robot's own battery percentage is out, and the pack voltage needs to become the source of truth.

Measuring the real battery

The plan is a pack-voltage monitor that reads the Ridgid pack directly, before the regulator, so the Jetson can see it actually going flat:

  • An ADS1115 16-bit ADC breakout on the Jetson's I2C bus, powered from 3.3 V.
  • A 100 kΩ / 15 kΩ divider scales the pack down by about 7.7×: a full 21 V pack reads as 2.74 V, safely inside the ADC's ±4.096 V range.
  • A 100 nF capacitor across the bottom resistor filters out motor noise.
  • Software warns at 16 V, then stops driving and shuts down cleanly at 15 V, about 3.0 V per cell.
Vpack = V_A0 × (100k + 15k) / 15k = V_A0 × 7.667
i2cdetect -y -r 7   # the ADS1115 should answer at 0x48

It's a stopgap until charging is fixed, but it works, and the pack is looked after by its own proper charger rather than by a robot with a known charging fault.

entry.title: Chasing “Charging Error 3”
entry.summary: The Roomba refused to charge. A service manual, a reconstructed schematic, a multimeter and two spare chargers later, the fault is cornered but not yet caught.
entry.content:
Every robot project has a detour. Mine started when I put the Roomba back on its charger and it refused, reporting Charging Error 3. This post is honest about where it ended: the fault is narrowed down, but not fixed. Yet.

What error 3 means

The 500-series service manual is short on detail but clear on this one: error 3 is a failed self-test of the charging MOSFETs. When charging starts, the robot briefly switches its charging transistors and checks that they behave. If the result isn't what the firmware expects, it gives up and shows error 3.

That points at a specific part of the board, which is a good start. It doesn't tell you which part.

Tracing the charge path

With no official schematic, I pieced one together from preliminary sketches, photos of the board and the markings on each part. Simplified, the charging current takes this route:

Q17 and Q18 are ZXMP6A17G P-channel MOSFETs, two switches in series between the charger and the battery. A P-channel MOSFET turns on when its gate is pulled several volts below its source. Small transistors marked “W2X” (most likely PMBT4401 NPNs: Q20 to Q23), plus a PMBT4403 PNP (Q12), do that pulling under the control of the robot's processor and a comparator that watches the charge current.

Measuring

With everything disconnected, I worked through the parts in the path with a multimeter in diode and resistance mode: the fuse, D58, the body diodes of Q17 and Q18, and each driver transistor's junctions. Annotated photos helped me keep track of which leg was which on parts smaller than a grain of rice.

Then the live measurements: with the charger connected, I measured the MOSFET gates relative to their sources to see whether the drivers were actually switching them. None of these checks turned up an obviously dead part.

Ruling out the easy answers

Before blaming the board, I swapped in a known-good battery, then a second charger. Error 3 stayed both times. That rules out the cheap fixes and puts the fault squarely in the robot's own charge-control circuitry.

Where it stands

The self-test lasts a fraction of a second. A multimeter averages over far longer than that, so it simply can't see what the gates are doing during the test. The next step is an oscilloscope on the gates and driver bases, triggered on the moment the charger is connected, to catch the self-test in the act.

Until then, the robot runs on a different power source entirely. That's the next post.

Please don't do the “obvious” fix

It's tempting to bridge the charging MOSFETs, or to charge the NiMH pack straight from a bench supply. Don't. Those FETs are how the robot stops charging when the pack is full; NiMH cells need proper end-of-charge detection, and overcharging them can make them vent or catch fire. Fix the circuit or use a real NiMH charger.

entry.title: Visual SLAM and navigation on a Roomba
entry.summary: From a stereo camera to a robot that explores rooms on its own: Basalt visual-inertial odometry, RTAB-Map, Nav2 and a web dashboard, plus five things that bit me along the way.
entry.content:
This is the post where the Roomba stops being a remote-control car and starts finding its own way around. Here's where it ended up: I press Explore & map, and it drives off into rooms it has never seen, building a map as it goes.

The pipeline

Robot navigation is a relay race. Each stage takes the previous one's output, adds something, and hands it on:

1. Where am I moving? Visual-inertial odometry

Basalt watches features in the stereo images, combines them with the camera's IMU, and estimates how the camera has moved, many times a second. It runs on the Jetson's CPU. It's impressively accurate until the camera stares at a blank wall or gets dazzled by a window, and then it loses track.

2. Bridging the gaps

So between Basalt and everything else sits a small watchdog node I wrote. While vision is healthy it passes the motion through. When tracking drops out, it bridges the gap with wheel odometry and the gyro, then hands back to vision once tracking recovers. The rest of the system never sees a jump.

3. The map: RTAB-Map

RTAB-Map takes that motion plus the depth images and builds the map. Its party trick is loop closure: when the robot comes back to somewhere it has been before and recognises it, RTAB-Map corrects all the drift that built up along the way and snaps the map straight.

4. Getting somewhere: Nav2

Nav2 turns the map into costmaps (where it's safe to drive and where it isn't), plans a path, and follows it with the Regulated Pure Pursuit controller, which slows down for tight turns and near obstacles. A collision monitor sits at the very end of the chain and will slow or stop the robot if anything gets too close, whatever the planner wants.

5. The dashboard

On top sits a small web app I can open on my phone: the live map, the camera feed, a drive pad, tap-to-go (tap a spot on the map and the robot plans its way there) and Explore & map, which hunts for frontiers, the edges between known and unknown space, and drives to them one by one until there's nothing left to discover.

Five things that bit me

  1. Sending Start drops you back to Passive. The OI's Start command (128) puts the robot in Passive mode, even if it was already in Safe mode. My driver re-sent Start when it reconnected, and the robot quietly stopped accepting drive commands. Now every Start is followed by the mode I actually want.
  2. One of my bumpers was lying. A stuck bumper switch reported a permanent collision, so the bump stop never let go. The driver can now be told to ignore a specific faulty sensor, rather than me ignoring safety altogether.
  3. Nav2's velocity polygons have to cover everything. In Nav2 Jazzy, the collision monitor's velocity polygons let you use a different safety zone at different speeds. Every combination of forward and turning speed the controller can command has to fall inside one of them. Leave a gap and the monitor misbehaves at exactly those speeds.
  4. Wheels lie on carpet. Turning on the spot, the wheel encoders claimed about 40% more rotation than actually happened: the wheels scrub sideways on carpet. The gyro and the visual odometry agreed with each other, so for rotation, they win.
  5. Don't chase frontiers you can't reach. The explorer kept choosing frontiers it could see through gaps, under furniture or between railings, but couldn't drive to. Goals now stop short of the frontier, in clear space the robot can actually reach.

Belt, braces and a bumper

Stairs and furniture don't forgive mistakes. The Roomba's own cliff sensors stay active in Safe mode, the collision monitor watches the depth camera, and the bump stop is the last resort. Three layers, because any one of them can be wrong.

The code: the launch files that wire this pipeline together are in roomba_bringup/launch, and the watchdog is vslam_watchdog.py, now also in Rust.

Next: an unexpected detour into the Roomba's charging circuit, in chasing Charging Error 3.

entry.title: Talking to the Roomba: serial wiring and a ROS 2 driver
entry.summary: The Roomba's 7-pin Mini-DIN port, why my first level-shifter wiring was flaky, the 5 V FT232 adapter that fixed it, and the open-source ROS 2 driver I wrote on top.
entry.content:
The ESP32 proved the Roomba would listen. Now the Jetson needed to hold a conversation with it for hours at a time, at full speed, without dropping a byte. That turned out to be harder than it sounds.

The port

The Open Interface lives on a 7-pin Mini-DIN socket under the Roomba's faceplate. Looking at the pins, this is what each one does:

PinNameWhat it does
1, 2VpwrBattery positive, unregulated (around 14–17 V). Do not connect.
3RXDSerial data into the Roomba (0–5 V)
4TXDSerial data out of the Roomba (0–5 V)
5BRCBaud rate change / wake-up input
6, 7GNDGround

Never connect pins 1 or 2 to your adapter

They carry raw battery voltage. A USB-serial adapter expects 5 V at most; 15-plus volts will destroy it, and possibly the USB port it's plugged into. Wire only RXD, TXD and ground (and BRC if you need it).

Attempt one: the Jetson's own UART

The Jetson has a hardware serial port on its 40-pin header, so the obvious plan was to use it. It runs at 3.3 V and the Roomba talks at 5 V, so I put a common BSS138 level-shifter board in between.

It mostly worked, which is the worst kind of working. Sensor packets would occasionally arrive corrupted, commands sometimes went missing, and the driver had to resynchronise on the data stream far too often. These bidirectional shifter boards rely on pull-up resistors to make their rising edges, and those soft edges are a known weak spot at 115200 baud. Rather than fight it, I changed the approach.

Attempt two: a 5 V FT232 adapter

An FT232 USB-to-TTL adapter with its voltage jumper set to 5 V speaks the Roomba's levels natively, so there's no level shifting at all. Plug it into the Jetson's USB port, connect TXD to the Roomba's RXD, RXD to TXD, and ground to ground, and talk at 115200 baud, 8N1.

It has been rock solid ever since: hours of streaming sensors and drive commands without a single framing error.

A ROS 2 driver

With a reliable link, I wrote a proper ROS 2 Jazzy driver and open-sourced it as roomba-serial-ros2. It does the boring-but-essential work so the rest of the robot doesn't have to know it's talking to a vacuum:

  • Drive: takes standard velocity commands and turns them into the Roomba's wheel-speed packets.
  • Odometry: reads the wheel encoder counts and publishes where the robot thinks it has moved.
  • Sensors and battery: bumpers, cliffs, wheel drops, voltage, current, charge and temperature, all as ROS topics. It also exposes the fun stuff: brushes, LEDs, the 4-digit display, songs and the dock button.
  • Safe and Full modes: it starts in Safe mode, which keeps the Roomba's own cliff protection active; Full mode hands over complete control when you really need it. On exit it hands the robot back in Passive mode.
  • Bump stop and a command watchdog: if a bumper triggers, or commands stop arriving, or the serial link drops, the wheels stop.
  • 36 unit tests: packet parsing, encoder wrap-around and mode handling are tested without needing a robot on the desk.
$ ros2 launch roomba_driver roomba_driver.launch.py
$ ros2 topic pub -r 10 /cmd_vel geometry_msgs/msg/Twist "{linear: {x: 0.1}}"
# Ctrl-C and the robot stops within half a second: no commands, no driving
$ ros2 topic echo /roomba/sensors

Things the manual doesn't tell you

A few findings from the real robot, all written up in the repository's troubleshooting notes:

  • 115200 baud, not 57600. The older SCI manual you'll find online is for pre-500 robots.
  • Safe mode is refused while the robot is lifted or sitting on its charger, and every motor command then earns you error beeps. Put it on the floor.
  • In Passive mode it falls asleep after five minutes, and streaming sensors doesn't keep it awake. Wiring the adapter's DTR line to BRC (pin 5) lets software wake it.
  • Trust the wheel encoders (packets 43 and 44). The firmware's own distance and angle packets were not reliable.
  • Don't stream everything at once. The full 84-byte sensor frame gave bad checksums in Safe mode; frames of 70 bytes or less are clean.

The repository also has the wiring diagrams, an Open Interface reference, and a small command-line tool for poking the robot without ROS at all. It's Apache-2.0 licensed, so help yourself if you have a 500-series Roomba of your own.

Update: the robot itself now runs a Rust port of this driver with the same topics, parameters and safety reflexes, at under a tenth of the CPU. More in From Python to Rust.

Next: giving it eyes, a map, and somewhere to go.

entry.title: Bringing a 2007-era Roomba 550 back as a robot platform
entry.summary: An old Roomba, an ESP32 and a published serial protocol: how a closet vacuum became the base for a mapping robot with a Jetson and a stereo camera.
entry.content:
My Roomba 550 is old enough to have its own nostalgia. It came out around 2007, it navigates by bumping into things, and for the last few years it has mostly lived in a closet. But it has one feature that makes it far more interesting than a newer robot vacuum: you can talk to it.

iRobot published the Roomba Open Interface (OI) for the 500 series. It's a simple serial protocol on a round port hidden under the top cover. Send it a few bytes and it will drive both wheels at any speed you like, play tones, run the brushes, and report every sensor it has: bumpers, cliff sensors, wheel drops, wheel encoder counts, the wall sensor, battery voltage, current and temperature. Underneath the vacuum is a perfectly good differential-drive robot base with a battery, motors and bump sensors, already paid for.

Step one: is it alive?

Before buying anything, I wanted proof that the robot would listen. An ESP32 was the quickest way to find out. A handful of lines of code later it was sending the OI start sequence, driving the Roomba forward, spinning it on the spot and printing sensor packets back to my laptop. Seeing a vacuum from 2007 obey a microcontroller is a very good feeling.

# the first bytes that made it move
128          Start: open the Open Interface
131          Safe mode: I drive, the cliff sensors still protect it
145 0 200 0 200   Drive Direct: right and left wheel at 200 mm/s

An ESP32 can drive a robot, though, and that's about it. It can't see. If I wanted the Roomba to know where it was, I needed real compute and real eyes.

The upgrade

Here's the hardware it carries now:

  • NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano Super (8 GB): a small Linux computer with a capable GPU, perfect for running computer vision on a robot's battery budget.
  • MYNT EYE D1000 stereo camera: two cameras for depth, an IR projector for blank walls, and a built-in IMU (gyro and accelerometer).
  • ROS 2 Jazzy: the Robot Operating System, which wires sensors, maps, planners and motors together as small cooperating programs.
  • A 3D-printed platform that bolts onto the top of the Roomba to carry the camera, the Jetson and the battery, while keeping the CLEAN button and the serial port reachable.

The goal

I want a robot that can:

  1. Map the house on its own using visual SLAM (simultaneous localisation and mapping): working out where it is from what the camera sees, while building the map at the same time.
  2. Avoid obstacles it can see, rather than finding them with its bumper.
  3. Become a smarter vacuum: clean the rooms I pick, in a sensible order, and know when it's done.

None of this needs a new robot. It needs some wiring, a lot of software, and patience. The rest of this build log is that story, mistakes included.

The code: the platform generator and its STLs are in hardware/platform.

Next up: getting a reliable serial link and writing a proper ROS 2 driver.
